title: How to Handle In-Laws (Leaving and Cleaving)
excerpt: Much marital misery is really an unfinished leaving. A man shall leave his father and mother, and we skip that verb in our hurry to the next one.
body:
The verse everyone knows says a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh. Three verbs, and we rush past the first two to get to the third. Leave. Hold fast. One flesh. The in-law trouble that strains so many marriages is almost always a failure at the first verb. Someone did not leave. They got married and stayed, in the ways that count, loyal to a parent in a way that left their spouse on the outside, and no amount of love at the third verb can fix a failure at the first.

This is not about loving your parents less. Honor your father and mother is a commandment that does not expire at the wedding. It is about reordering, about a new primary loyalty being formed, a new household that the old loyalties now arrange themselves around rather than rule.

## What leaving actually means

Leaving is not geographic and it is not the end of the relationship with your parents. It is a shift in allegiance. Before marriage your primary human loyalty was to the family you came from. After marriage it is to the spouse. This means that when there is a conflict between your parent's wishes and your marriage's good, the marriage wins, and your parent does not get a vote that outranks your spouse's.

You can tell whether someone has left by what happens under pressure. When the mother criticizes the wife, does the husband defend his wife or fall silent and let it stand. When the father disapproves of a decision the couple made together, does the son hold the line with his spouse or quietly side with his father and leave his wife exposed. The spouse who has not left keeps siding, in the small moments, with the family of origin, and the married spouse feels it as a betrayal even when nothing dramatic is said, because they have learned they are not actually first.

## The unleft spouse, and the one married to them

If you are the one who has not fully left, the tell is usually a particular fear, the fear of your parent's disappointment. You make decisions, or fail to make them, to avoid a mother's hurt look or a father's cooled approval, and your spouse pays for it. The work here is to grow up the rest of the way, to be able to disappoint your parent for the sake of your marriage without it feeling like the end of the world. That is what leaving costs, and it is a cost you have to be willing to pay, repeatedly, in small moments, until your spouse knows without question that they come first.

If you are married to someone who has not left, the temptation is to fight the in-laws directly, and it almost always backfires, because attacking your spouse's parent forces them to choose, and a person who has not finished leaving will instinctively defend the parent. The wiser move is to aim at your spouse, gently, not at the parent. Not your mother is impossible, which makes him defensive, but I need to know that you and I decide things together, and that when it matters, you are on my side. Make it about the loyalty, not about the parent's character. The goal is to help your spouse leave, not to win a war against their family.

## Set the boundary together, present it as one

The single most important practical rule with in-laws is that the boundary is set by the couple together and presented as a united front, and ideally communicated by the spouse whose parent it is. The husband talks to his parents. The wife talks to hers. This protects everyone. It keeps the in-law from feeling attacked by the outsider who married in, and it forces the couple to decide together rather than one spouse managing the other's family alone.

When the boundary gets crossed, the parent should hear it from their own child, not from the in-law. Mom, we have decided we are doing our own Christmas morning this year, and we will come over in the afternoon. From the son, that is a family reordering. From the daughter-in-law, it is an insult and a power struggle. Same boundary, completely different result, depending on who carries it.

## A few common fault lines

The holidays are the classic battleground, two families each assuming they get the couple, and the couple torn in half trying to satisfy both. The answer is that the new household decides its own holidays and then informs the families, kindly and clearly and early, rather than asking permission and getting trapped between two sets of expectations.

Money from parents is another quiet trap, because money often comes with strings, spoken or not, and a couple dependent on a parent's generosity can find that the parent has bought a vote in the marriage. Receive help with open eyes. If the gift comes with control attached, the gift may cost more than it gives.

And the criticism of a spouse by a parent is the one that wounds longest. A parent who runs down your spouse to you is asking you to betray your marriage, even if they would never call it that. The leaving spouse does not laugh along or stay silent. They say, gently and once, that is my husband, my wife, you are talking about, and I need you to speak about them with respect. You defend the absent spouse to your own family. That is what holding fast looks like when they are not in the room.

## Honor without obeying

None of this is permission to dishonor your parents. You can honor a parent and still not obey them, still not let them rule a marriage they are not part of. Honor means respect, care, presence, gratitude, the cup of cold water in their old age. It does not mean the surrendering of your marriage's authority to them. Jesus himself, at the wedding in Cana, gently set a boundary with his own mother while still honoring her. The two are not enemies. A grown child can hold a parent in deep love and still make unmistakably clear where their first loyalty now lies.

## This week

Have one conversation with your spouse, alone, with no in-law in the room. Ask each other a single honest question: is there any place where you feel I have not fully left, where you feel my family comes before you. Then listen without defending, because the defending is the very reflex that proves the point. Pick one boundary you have both wanted and have been afraid to set, and agree that the spouse whose parent it is will carry it, kindly and clearly, this week. Leaving is not a one-time act at the altar. It is a thousand small moments of choosing your spouse out loud, and your marriage will know, by the end of this week, whether you are willing to do it.
